tracks.title: The Country Diary of a Subway Conductor

essay:
Two guys named Dan started a record label in Chicago in 1989 because they were record-store clerks who couldn't stop buying weird 7"s. Dan Koretzky and Dan Osborn bonded over underground music and decided to just start a label — Drag City. Neither of them had any money. What they had was taste, and for the first five years that taste built, almost by accident, one of the most important rosters in American underground music.

Drag City's catalog number DC1 is Royal Trux's 'Hero Zero,' a 1990 7" that actually sold — funding the label's second release: Pavement's 'Demolition Plot J-7,' recorded in Gary Young's home studio in Stockton.

By 1992-93 the roster widened into a Chicago-Louisville family tree. Will Oldham recruited three-quarters of the recently-disbanded Slint to back him on Palace Brothers' debut. Bill Callahan, recording as Smog, made his first studio album, 'Julius Caesar.' David Grubbs folded his post-hardcore band into Gastr del Sol. And David Berman — friends with Malkmus and Nastanovich since college — started sending Koretzky cassette tapes as Silver Jews, resulting in 'Starlite Walker.'

Every one of these records was made by people who barely had money, barely had gear, and had zero commercial ambition — and every single one ended up mattering more than almost anything else released in American indie rock in the following decade.
